lesson.title: Connected things, safely
lesson.subtitle: What the Internet of Things is, and how to stay safe

video.title: Connected things, safely
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Dr Farah holding a phone that shows a grainy live view of a small shop at night; a small camera on the shop wall.
scenes.animation: The live view flickers on; a red dot blinks.
scenes.narration: My cousin bought a cheap camera to watch her shop at night. A week later, a friend sent her a link. It was her shop, live, on a website anyone could open. She'd never changed the camera's password.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: the Internet of Things, and how to stay safe with it.

scenes.visual: An everyday object, a water tank, opens up to show a sensor, a tiny chip and a small antenna, with radio waves going out.
scenes.animation: Each part lights up in turn; waves ripple from the antenna.
scenes.narration: The Internet of Things means everyday things connected to a network. Each one has three parts: a sensor to notice, a small computer to decide, and a connection to send and receive.

scenes.visual: Four quick panels: a living room, a school roof with a weather station, a bus on a phone map, a farm field with a sensor on a stick.
scenes.animation: Panels slide in one by one.
scenes.narration: At home: a smart TV, a gate camera, a watch that counts steps. At school: a weather station that sends readings. In town: buses you can follow on a map. On farms: soil sensors that text the farmer.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma on the school roof beside a small weather station with a rain cup and a thermometer box. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Our school's weather station has sensors for rain and heat, and a small computer. What would make it part of the Internet of Things?

scenes.visual: The weather station sends little packets through the air to a phone in a teacher's hand, far across town.
scenes.animation: Packets travel along a dotted path; the phone lights up.
scenes.narration: A connection that sends its readings. Sensors and a small computer make a clever gadget. Add Wi-Fi, a mobile network or a radio link, and the readings reach a phone far away.

scenes.visual: A box labelled 'admin' on a new camera; a long list of passwords scrolls past; many small cameras and routers on a map turn red.
scenes.animation: The list scrolls; dots across the map turn red one after another.
scenes.narration: Remember that shop camera? Many devices leave the factory with an easy password, like admin. Attackers keep lists of them. In twenty sixteen, a program called Mirai used about sixty of them to take over hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers.

scenes.visual: A student and a parent set up a new router: a new password typed, an update bar filling, a switch turned off.
scenes.animation: Each step ticks as it is done.
scenes.narration: So, with an adult, make every new device safe. Change the factory password to a long new one. Turn on updates, which fix weak spots. And switch off features you don't use.

scenes.visual: A phone shows a permission box: 'Torch wants to read your contacts'. A thumb hovers, then taps Don't allow.
scenes.animation: The box pops up; the thumb taps; a settings gear spins.
scenes.narration: Apps ask for permissions: your camera, microphone, location or contacts. Before you tap Allow, ask: does it need this for its job? A torch app needs the flash, not your contacts. You can change permissions any time.

scenes.visual: A photo with a small map pin hidden in its corner; a watch drawing a line from a home to a school.
scenes.animation: The pin pops out of the photo; the line draws itself.
scenes.narration: Connected things share, too. A photo can carry the place it was taken. A fitness watch can map your walk to school. So share less, and keep accounts private.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a phone with three permission boxes stacked on a puzzle game. Three answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A free puzzle game asks for your microphone, your contacts and your location. What do you allow?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a sensor with waves, a key, a permission switch, a lock.
scenes.narration: None of them: a puzzle needs no microphone, contacts or location. Remember: the Internet of Things is things that sense, decide and connect. Change factory passwords and keep devices updated. Allow only what an app needs, and share less.

scenes.visual: A student and a grandparent at a table with a list: router, TV, phones. A tick beside 'password changed'.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: with an adult, list the connected things at home, from the router to the TV. Was each one's factory password ever changed? Then open one app's permissions, and switch off one it doesn't need.

checkpoints.prompt: A weather station has sensors and a small computer. What would put it on the Internet of Things?

options.text: More sensors, for wind and sunlight
A bigger screen to show the readings
A connection that sends its readings

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it already senses and decides. A connection that sends its readings over a network puts it on the Internet of Things.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — sensors and a computer make a clever gadget, not a connected one. What's missing is a connection that sends the readings over a network.

checkpoints.prompt: A free puzzle game asks for your microphone, contacts and location. What do you allow?

options.text: All three, or the game won't work
None: a puzzle needs none of them
Just location: that one is harmless

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a puzzle needs none of them. Tap Don't allow: most games still work, and your voice, contacts and location stay yours.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a puzzle game needs none of them, and location isn't harmless: it shows where you live and study. Tap Don't allow; most games still work.
